details:
**Helena**
The capital of Montana, in the west-central part of the state. It began as a gold-rush town in the 1860s and is the giveaway at the end of almost every question.

**Glacier National Park and Going-to-the-Sun Road**
Montana's most famous national park, in the northern Rockies along the Canadian border. Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the park over Logan Pass, passing Lake McDonald, Heavens Peak, and Saint Mary Lake. Stanley Kubrick filmed the opening shots of The Shining along Saint Mary Lake. With Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park, Glacier forms the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park.

**Triple Divide Peak**
A mountain in Glacier National Park where the Continental (Great) Divide meets the Northern (Laurentian) Divide. Rain falling on it can drain to the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic (through the Gulf of Mexico), or Hudson Bay and the Arctic.

**Butte, the Berkeley Pit, and Anaconda Copper**
Butte, in Silver Bow County, was a booming copper-mining city run by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was the home of the "Copper King" William A. Clark, whose mansion still stands there. The city is named for a nearby flat-topped hill (a butte). The abandoned Berkeley Pit, a former open-pit copper mine, is now filled with toxic, highly acidic water and is a Superfund site.

**Great Falls**
Montana's third-largest city, on the Missouri River. It is named for the series of waterfalls, including Black Eagle Falls and Rainbow Falls, that Lewis and Clark had to carry their boats around in 1805. The falls appear on the state seal.

**Source of the Missouri River (Three Forks)**
In southwest Montana, near Three Forks, the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin rivers join to form the Missouri River. Lewis and Clark named all three rivers in 1805.

**Fort Peck Dam**
A huge earth-fill dam on the Missouri River in northeast Montana, south of Glasgow, built in the 1930s as a New Deal project. It created Fort Peck Lake, one of the largest reservoirs in the U.S., which also floods the lower Musselshell River.

**Bitterroot Mountains and Trapper Peak**
The Bitterroot Range of the Rockies forms much of Montana's western border with Idaho. Trapper Peak is the highest summit in the range.

**Little Bighorn (Battle of the Greasy Grass)**
In 1876, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors wiped out George Armstrong Custer's detachment of the 7th Cavalry at the Little Bighorn River in southeast Montana, known as "Custer's Last Stand." Major Marcus Reno led a separate attack that was driven back. Native peoples call it the Battle of the Greasy Grass. The battlefield is on the Crow Indian Reservation.

**Chief Joseph and the Nez Perce**
In 1877 the Nez Perce, led by Chief Joseph, fled U.S. troops on a long journey toward Canada. They surrendered in the Bear Paw Mountains of northern Montana, just short of the border, where Joseph reportedly said, "I will fight no more forever."

**Billings, Missoula, and Bozeman**
Billings is Montana's largest city, and Pictograph Cave, with its ancient rock paintings, is nearby. Missoula is home to the University of Montana. Bozeman is home to Montana State University and the Museum of the Rockies, known for its dinosaur fossils.

**Flathead Lake and Kalispell**
Flathead Lake in northwest Montana is the largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi in the contiguous United States. The city of Kalispell lies just north of it, and the resort town of Whitefish lies west of Glacier National Park.

**Granite Peak**
The highest point in Montana, about 12,800 feet, in the Beartooth Mountains near the Wyoming border. Froze-to-Death Mountain and its plateau are nearby.

**Only state bordering Alberta ("Big Sky Country")**
Montana borders three Canadian provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. It is the only U.S. state that touches Alberta. Its nickname is "Big Sky Country," and it also contains a small northern strip of Yellowstone National Park.

**A River Runs Through It**
Norman Maclean's 1976 novella about brothers who fly-fish near Missoula. The novella and Robert Redford's 1992 film adaptation helped popularize fly fishing in Montana.
